🇺🇸🇮🇷 Prof. Mohammad Marandi: Iran is ready to strike first if it believes an American attack is coming.

I spoke with Professor Mohammad Marandi in Tehran as Iran's military leadership issued some of its strongest warnings yet to Washington.

Iranian commanders say they are monitoring US and Israeli military preparations and could launch attacks BEFORE incoming strikes begin, potentially against American interests far beyond the Middle East.

Marandi made an important distinction.

Iran doesn't consider the war over. He says there is no formal ceasefire, and Tehran has no intention of waiting for American missiles to start falling if it detects an imminent operation.

But he also believes Trump still has a way out.

According to Marandi, Iran remains willing to reach an agreement through the existing diplomatic framework. He thinks the next 48 hours could be particularly important, with the U.S. midterms approaching and financial markets under pressure.

We also discussed the possibility of attacks on American warships, Gulf energy infrastructure and countries hosting U.S. forces.

Marandi warned that if Washington begins targeting Iran's civilian infrastructure, Tehran's response could become much broader.

Then our conversation took a rather different turn.

We debated Ehud Olmert, Israel's conduct in Lebanon and Gaza, allegations circulating about Iran and Yemen, and whether journalists can responsibly report claims from opposing sides without independently establishing their accuracy.

Marandi challenged me directly over our coverage. I pushed back on the practical difficulties of verifying information during a war.

Iran isn't planning to surrender under military pressure. Trump can still negotiate, but Marandi believes another attack would trigger a much wider confrontation.

That's his assessment, not confirmation that either side has decided to strike.

@s_m_marandi

Judge James Boasberg keeps landing the most politically explosive cases against the Trump administration — and lawmakers want to know why.

The Obama-appointed chief judge of D.C. District Court is now overseeing the fight to unseal Rep. Ilhan Omar's search warrant, on top of California's voter-roll lawsuit, the deportation flights dispute that reached the Supreme Court, and the Signal messages case involving top Trump officials. Reps. Jim Jordan, Darrell Issa, and Chip Roy sent a letter to the court clerk demanding answers about how cases are assigned, writing that they "cannot independently verify the randomness of case assignments because the composition of assignment decks is kept secret."

Sen. Eric Schmitt has introduced legislation — literally named the Boasberg Act — that would require federal courts to assign cases randomly without exceptions. It's stalled in committee.

🇺🇲 🇧🇷 Washington's position on Flavio Bolsonaro came into sharper focus on Saturday.

Speaking to reporters at a Halloween event at Mar-a-Lago, President Trump said he had no plans to meet the defeated Brazilian candidate but that he "got treated very shabbily." "He can stay here as long as he wants. The election was a disgrace," Trump said. On Thursday he had also described Brazil's vote as a disgrace and declined to say whom he regards as Brazil's legitimate president. He has not congratulated Lula, who won the October 25 runoff by about 4.43 million votes, a result confirmed by the electoral court and accepted by Bolsonaro's Liberal Party.

In Atlanta, where he hosted the G20 foreign ministers, Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected reports that the administration helped Bolsonaro leave Brazil. "We didn't facilitate anything," he said. "We had word that he had arrived in the United States. He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country." Rubio said the government was not "involved directly in any of the moves that were made," and that Trump "made clear that if he arrived in the United States at a port of entry, that he would be paroled into the country, and he was."

⚠️ The denial is narrow. It addresses the departure, which The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal reported involved a private jet arranged by White House aide Jason Miller, while confirming a presidential decision on entry. Reports describe a one-year humanitarian parole, though the State Department earlier spoke of visas. Parole is a discretionary, temporary status and does not amount to asylum.

Bolsonaro left Brazil despite a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports. He faces separate financial investigations, denies wrongdoing and has not been charged.

Brasilia has chosen restraint. According to Brazilian media citing officials, Itamaraty advised Lula not to respond publicly and to treat the case as a judicial matter. Rubio said he saw Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday. Brazilian diplomats reportedly expect a clearer US position after Tuesday's midterm elections.
